name: Venice
subtitle: The City in the Lagoon
description: Venice and its lagoon from the first doges at Rivoalto to the fall of the Republic in 1797: the islands round the Grand Canal, San Marco and the Rialto, the Arsenal to the east, Cannaregio and the Ghetto to the north-west, the Giudecca and San Giorgio across the water to the south. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Canal Grande
water.blurb: An old river channel winding through the islands in a reversed S, about 3.8 km long, 30–70 m wide and some 5 m deep. It was the city's main street: every great family built its palazzo with a water-gate on it, and until 1854 the Rialto was its only bridge.

water.name: Canale di Cannaregio
water.blurb: The second canal of the city and the old way in from the mainland: boats from Mestre and the rivers of the Veneto came this way before the railway bridge of 1846.

water.name: Rio della Misericordia
water.blurb: One of the three parallel canals of northern Cannaregio, dug as the marsh here was reclaimed in the 13th and 14th centuries, with the Scuola Grande della Misericordia on its bank.

water.name: Rio della Sensa
water.blurb: The northernmost of the Cannaregio canals, lined with modest houses, gardens and the church of Madonna dell'Orto, where Tintoretto lived and is buried.

water.name: Rio di San Trovaso
water.blurb: A canal from the Grand Canal down to the Zattere, with one of the last working squeri, the boatyard of San Trovaso, on its bank.

water.name: Rio di San Barnaba
water.blurb: A canal through Dorsoduro from the Grand Canal toward the Zattere, crossed by the Ponte dei Pugni where the factions fought for the bridge.

water.name: Rio di Palazzo
water.blurb: The narrow canal behind the Doge's Palace, between the palace and its prisons, running north past the canons' houses of San Marco.

water.name: Rio dei Mendicanti
water.blurb: The canal from the campo of Santi Giovanni e Paolo north to the lagoon, along the flank of the Scuola Grande di San Marco and the hospital of the Mendicanti.

water.name: Rio dell'Arsenale
water.blurb: The canal from the basin of San Marco to the water gate of the Arsenal, between two towers; every galley built inside came out this way.

water.name: Canale di San Pietro
water.blurb: The channel round the island of San Pietro di Castello, the ancient Olivolo, seat of the bishops of Venice from the 8th century and of the patriarch until 1807.

water.name: Rio Batario
water.blurb: A canal that crossed the later Piazza in front of the church of San Geminiano. Doge Sebastiano Ziani had it filled in about 1172–78 to make the Piazza the size it is now.

water.name: Harbour of the doge's castle
water.blurb: Where the Piazzetta is now, a small harbour came up to the walls of the doge's castle; the reconstruction is uncertain, based on excavations and old descriptions.

water.name: Rio di Sant'Elena
water.blurb: The channel between Castello and the island of Sant'Elena, with its convent of Olivetan monks and their meadows.

water.name: Canale della Giudecca
water.blurb: The deep channel, 300–400 m wide, between the Zattere and the Giudecca, the way in for ships coming from the port of Malamocco. Timber rafts (zattere) once moored along the quay that took their name.

water.name: Laguna Veneta
water.blurb: A shallow tidal lagoon about 50 km long behind the sand bars of the Lido and Pellestrina, mostly under a metre deep at low tide. Its channels were the city's streets and walls: the Republic dredged them, marked them with stakes and diverted whole rivers to keep the lagoon from silting up.

roads.name: Path from Rivoalto to San Marco
Mercerie
roads.blurb: The chain of shopping streets from the clock tower to the Rialto, the city's high street: silk, spices, glass, books and jewels sold from ground-floor shops under the signs of their makers.

roads.name: Ruga degli Orefici and Ruga Vecchia
roads.blurb: From the foot of the Rialto bridge past the goldsmiths' arcades to Campo San Polo and on toward the Frari: the main walk of the San Polo side.

roads.name: Riva degli Schiavoni
roads.blurb: The quay along the basin of San Marco, named after the Dalmatian (Slav) sailors and merchants who moored here. Ships unloaded at the Riva into the 18th century; it was paved in stone and widened in 1780–82.

roads.name: Salizada San Lio and Ruga Giuffa
Calle Larga San Moisè and Santo Stefano
Calli of Santi Apostoli, Santa Fosca and San Marcuola
Fondamenta delle Zattere
roads.blurb: The long quay facing the Giudecca, paved in 1519, where timber rafts floated down from the Alps were moored and broken up; salt warehouses and boatyards lined it.

roads.name: Fondamente Nove
roads.blurb: The 'new quays' built from 1589 along the northern edge of the city, looking out over the lagoon to San Michele and Murano.

bridges.name: Ponte della Moneta (bridge of boats)
bridges.blurb: A bridge of boats laid across the Grand Canal about 1181, traditionally credited to Nicolò Barattieri; the tolls went to the mint, hence its name.

bridges.name: Ponte di Rialto (timber)
bridges.blurb: The timber bridge with shops and a central drawbridge that could be raised for masted ships. It collapsed under a crowd in 1444 and was rebuilt the same way.

bridges.name: Ponte di Rialto
bridges.blurb: Antonio da Ponte's single stone arch of 1588–91, 28 m wide, carrying three streets and two rows of shops.

bridges.name: Ponte della Paglia
bridges.blurb: The bridge on the Riva over the Rio di Palazzo, named, it is said, after the barges of straw that moored here; rebuilt in stone in 1360.

bridges.name: Ponte dei Sospiri
bridges.blurb: The covered bridge of 1600–03 between the palace and the New Prisons. The 'sighs' are a Romantic invention of the 19th century.

bridges.name: Ponte delle Guglie
bridges.blurb: The bridge over the Cannaregio canal near its mouth on the Grand Canal: of timber from 1285, rebuilt in stone in 1580 and named after the obelisks at its corners.

bridges.name: Ponte dei Tre Archi
bridges.blurb: The only three-arched bridge in Venice, built over the Cannaregio canal in 1688 by Andrea Tirali.

bridges.name: Ponte dei Pugni
bridges.blurb: The 'bridge of the fists': without parapets, it was a battleground where Castellani and Nicolotti fought to push each other into the canal, until the fights were banned in 1705. Marble footprints mark the starting places.

blocks.name: San Zaccaria and Santa Maria Formosa

marsh.name: Marshes of Castello and the Zemelle

districts.name: Cannaregio
districts.description: The northern sestiere, named after the canal of reeds (canne) that leads into it: parish churches, long fondamente, the Ghetto, gardens and the houses of boatmen and artisans.

districts.name: San Marco
districts.description: The sestiere of government and money: the Piazza, the Doge's Palace, the Mercerie and the richest shops, inside the last bend of the Grand Canal.

districts.name: Castello
districts.description: The eastern sestiere, named after the castle of Olivolo: the cathedral of San Pietro, the Arsenal and the dense parishes of its shipwrights, sailors and Dalmatian and Greek merchants.

districts.name: San Polo and Santa Croce
districts.description: The two sestieri on the inside of the Grand Canal's great bend, from the Rialto market to the western edge of the city, with the Frari and the Scuola of San Rocco.

districts.name: Dorsoduro
districts.description: The 'hard back', the firmest ground of the islands, from the Punta della Dogana to the fishermen's parish of San Nicolò dei Mendicoli; the Giudecca belonged to it.

periods.label: Rivoalto
periods.summary: In 810–811 the doges moved their seat from Malamocco to the islets of Rivoalto, safer from the Franks. Around 900 Venice is a scatter of muddy islets in the lagoon, each with its parish church, timber houses, boatyards, salt and fish. The doge lives in a fortified castle by the water; beside it his chapel holds the body of Saint Mark, stolen from Alexandria in 828.
periods.feel: Reeds hissing on the mudflats, the slap of oars, woodsmoke from timber houses, gulls over the fish baskets at the Rialto landing.

houses.title: Timber houses on the islets
houses.text: Houses of wood and wattle on piles and rubble footings, thatched or shingled, one or two storeys round a yard with a rain-cistern, a boat tied at the door. Only the churches and the doge's castle are of brick and stone.

outskirts.title: Mudflats, salt pans and orchards
outskirts.text: Barene (salt marsh) cut by creeks, fish ponds, salt pans, vineyards and kitchen gardens round the parish churches. Firewood, lime and stone all came by boat from the mainland.

periods.label: The Crusaders' Venice
periods.summary: Enrico Dandolo's Venice: a sea power with quarters in Constantinople and the ports of the east. Doge Sebastiano Ziani (1172–78) has laid out the Piazza and rebuilt the palace; the new San Marco, consecrated in 1094, is being clad in marble and in loot from Constantinople after 1204. The Rialto is the market of the city, reached by a bridge of boats; the Arsenal builds the state's galleys.
periods.feel: Shipwrights' mallets, Greek and Arabic on the quays, pepper, wax and cotton swung ashore at the Rialto, the bells of some sixty parishes.

houses.title: Byzantine-style merchants' houses
houses.text: Merchants' houses of brick with a water-gate on the canal, a ground-floor warehouse behind an arcaded portico and a long hall above, stilted round arches trimmed in white Istrian stone. Ordinary houses are still largely of timber.

outskirts.title: Islets still being made
outskirts.text: Gardens, vineyards, boatyards and marsh at the edges of the islands. New land is made by driving piles, building a wall of planks and filling behind it with mud, rubble and rubbish.

periods.label: The Lagoon Republic
periods.summary: One of Europe's largest and richest cities, ruled since 1297 by the closed patriciate of the Great Council. The Gothic lagoon wing of the Doge's Palace is finished; the friars' churches of the Frari and Santi Giovanni e Paolo are rising in brick. Convoys of state galleys sail from the enlarged Arsenal to Alexandria, Beirut and Flanders. Venice has come through the Black Death and the war of Chioggia.
periods.population: about 85,000–110,000, recovering from the plague of 1348
periods.feel: Boatmen's cries at blind corners, spices and hot pitch on the air, bells everywhere, Latin, German, Greek and Tuscan in the crowd at the Rialto.

houses.title: Gothic houses and palazzi
houses.text: Brick houses of three storeys, plastered and coloured, with pointed windows in white Istrian stone, a water-gate and a portego (hall) running through each floor, funnel chimneys and tiled roofs; rows of small terrace houses for artisans and sailors.

outskirts.title: Gardens and squeri
outskirts.text: Walled convent gardens and orchards, boatyards (squeri) with their slipways, rope-walks and timber stacks at the city's edges, above all in Castello, northern Cannaregio and on the Giudecca.

periods.label: Renaissance Venice
periods.summary: After the shock of Agnadello (1509) and the Portuguese spice route, Venice builds in stone: Sansovino's Library and Loggetta on the Piazza, Palladio's San Giorgio and, after the plague of 1575–77, his Redentore. The Ghetto (1516) encloses the Jews; printers, glassmakers and silk weavers fill the city. The Rialto bridge is still of wood: its stone successor follows in 1588–91.
periods.population: about 170,000 before the plague of 1575–77, which killed perhaps a quarter to a third
periods.feel: Presses thumping, gold leaf and incense, courtesans' perfume, the Arsenal bell calling two thousand workers at dawn.

houses.title: Palazzi and terrace houses
houses.text: Tall houses of brick and Istrian stone, up to five storeys in the crowded centre, with balconies and wooden roof terraces (altane); classical palazzi on the Grand Canal; long rows of identical rented houses built by the scuole and the state for workers and widows.

outskirts.title: Orchards, convents and the Giudecca
outskirts.text: Convent gardens, patrician pleasure gardens on the Giudecca, timber and boat yards on the Zattere, vegetable plots in the far corners of Cannaregio and Castello.

periods.label: The Last Years of the Serenissima
periods.summary: A city of pleasure and slow decline: the Republic is neutral and shrinking, but Carnival lasts for months, the Piazza is the salon of Europe and theatres and casinos run all night. The Salute (1631–87) closes the view down the Grand Canal; the Rialto has been of stone since 1591. On 12 May 1797 the Great Council votes itself out of existence before Napoleon's army.
periods.feel: Masked crowds in the Piazza, coffee and chocolate under the arcades, violins from the girls' choirs of the ospedali, black gondolas waiting in rows.

houses.title: Refaced houses and rented palazzi
houses.text: Old Gothic houses refaced and plastered in ochre, pink and white, storeys added on top, balconies with iron railings; patrician palazzi let out by the floor. The poor live in damp ground-floor rooms that flood at acqua alta.

outskirts.title: Gardens and boatyards
outskirts.text: Kitchen gardens and vineyards in Castello and on the Giudecca, convents behind high walls, timber yards and squeri, the meadows and convent of Sant'Elena.

landmarks.name: Basilica di San Marco

early-900.name: First church of San Marco
early-900.note: The doge's chapel built 828–832 for the body of Saint Mark, stolen from Alexandria in 828. Burnt in 976 and repaired by Pietro I Orseolo; its form is known only from excavated foundations.

dandolo-1204.name: San Marco (Contarini church)
dandolo-1204.note: The third church, begun about 1063 and consecrated in 1094, on the plan of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople: five low brick domes. Marble revetment, columns and the loot of 1204 are being added.

republic-1400.note: Clad in marble, with the tall lead outer domes raised in the 13th century and the four bronze horses on the loggia. The Gothic crown of ogee arches and saints is being added round 1400.

cinquecento-1580.note: Complete as it would stand for centuries: gold mosaics inside and in the lunettes, the horses over the main door, the Gothic crown and the three bronze flagpole bases (1505) in front.

serenissima-1780.note: Still the doge's private chapel, not the cathedral. In 1797 the French take the horses to Paris; they come back in 1815.

landmarks.summary: The doge's chapel and shrine of Saint Mark: a Greek cross of brick clad in marble, with five domes, a front of five portals and gold mosaics, and the bronze horses from Constantinople.
details: The present church was begun about 1063 and consecrated in 1094 on the model of Justinian's Holy Apostles in Constantinople: a Greek cross with a dome over the centre and each arm, 76 m long and 62 m wide. After 1204 its brick was sheathed in marble and spolia, the low domes were raised with timber-and-lead outer shells and the façade received its horses and its Gothic crown.

The miniature shows the church after about 1420: narthex and five portals, the loggia with the horses, five upper arches with ogee crowns and pinnacles, the five lead domes with lanterns. The north (Zen chapel, treasury) and south annexes are simplified; mosaics are flat gold panels.
landmarks.function: Doge's chapel and shrine of Saint Mark

landmarks.name: Campanile di San Marco

early-900.note: A watchtower may already have been begun here about 900, under Doge Pietro Tribuno; the evidence is late and uncertain.

dandolo-1204.note: The brick bell tower finished in the 12th century, its belfry topped by a pyramid spire; a lookout and lighthouse for ships coming in from the Lido.

republic-1400.note: Struck again and again by lightning; the wooden spire burns in 1489 and is rebuilt only in 1511–14.

cinquecento-1580.note: Rebuilt 1511–14 by Bartolomeo Bon: belfry of white arches, an attic with lions of Saint Mark, a green pyramid and a gilded angel. At its foot Sansovino's Loggetta (1537–49).

serenissima-1780.note: 98.6 m high, the tallest building in the city; Galileo showed the Senate his telescope from the belfry in 1609. It collapsed in 1902 and was rebuilt exactly by 1912.

landmarks.summary: The bell tower of San Marco, 98.6 m: a plain brick shaft with a white belfry, a pyramid spire and a gilded angel, with Sansovino's Loggetta at its foot.
details: Begun as a watchtower in the 9th or 10th century and completed as a bell tower in the 12th, the campanile was rebuilt from the belfry up by Bartolomeo Bon in 1511–14 after lightning destroyed the spire in 1489. Its five bells marked the working day, the sessions of the councils and executions.

The miniature shows the 16th-century tower: the shaft with its pilaster strips, the belfry loggia, the attic with reliefs, the green copper pyramid and the angel, and the marble Loggetta on its east side. The earlier variant has a simpler belfry and a squat spire, a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Palazzo Ducale

early-900.name: Castle of the doges
early-900.note: The doge's seat since about 811: a castle with corner towers and walls by the water, its harbour where the Piazzetta is now. Burnt with San Marco in the revolt of 976.

dandolo-1204.name: Palace of Sebastiano Ziani
dandolo-1204.note: Rebuilt by Doge Sebastiano Ziani (1172–78) as an open Byzantine-style palace with arcaded wings round a court; the old towers survive at the corners.

republic-1400.note: The Gothic lagoon wing with the Great Council hall (begun 1340) stands complete; its balcony window is carved in 1404. The Piazzetta wing is still Ziani's, rebuilt to match from 1424.

cinquecento-1580.note: Both Gothic façades are finished, with the Porta della Carta (1438–42) and Rizzo's courtyard wing after the fire of 1483. Fires in 1574 and 20 December 1577 gut the council halls.

serenissima-1780.note: The government of the Republic at work for its last years: councils, courts, the prisons across the Bridge of Sighs. The Great Council meets here for the last time on 12 May 1797.

landmarks.summary: The seat of the doge and of every council and court of the Republic: two Gothic façades of open arcades and loggias carrying a wall of pink and white marble lozenges.
details: A castle in the 9th century, an open palace under Ziani, the building took its present form from 1340, when the Great Council voted a new hall over the lagoon: 54 m long, one of the largest rooms in Europe. The Piazzetta wing followed from 1424. The upside-down look, lace below and solid wall above, is Venice's own.

The miniature shows the palace after about 1440: 17 arches on the lagoon and 18 on the Piazzetta, the loggia of pointed arches and quatrefoils, the diamond-patterned upper wall with its great windows and balconies, the crenellation of white merlons, and the Renaissance east wing on the Rio di Palazzo.
landmarks.function: Palace of the doge, councils, courts and prisons

landmarks.name: Piazza San Marco

early-900.note: The brolo, an orchard of the nuns of San Zaccaria, with the church of San Geminiano and the Rio Batario crossing it in front of San Marco.

dandolo-1204.note: Laid out by Doge Sebastiano Ziani about 1172–78: the Rio Batario filled in, San Geminiano rebuilt at the far end, the space doubled. Paved in brick in herringbone, according to the chronicles in 1264.

republic-1400.note: Brick herringbone with bands of white stone; markets, processions and tournaments are held here.

cinquecento-1580.note: Three bronze flagpole bases by Alessandro Leopardi (1505) stand before the basilica; Sansovino rebuilt San Geminiano at the far end in 1557.

serenissima-1780.note: Repaved in 1723 to Andrea Tirali's design: grey trachyte with bands of white Istrian stone. The salon of Europe: cafés, puppet shows, charlatans and masks.

landmarks.summary: The great square of Venice, about 175 m long, enclosed by the Procuratie and closed at the west end by the church of San Geminiano, with the basilica at its head.
details: The only space in Venice called a piazza; every other square is a campo. Doge Sebastiano Ziani doubled it by filling a canal about 1172–78, and the Procuratie were rebuilt around it in the 16th and 17th centuries. Napoleon pulled down San Geminiano in 1807 to build the wing that now closes the west end.

The miniature shows the paving (brick herringbone before 1723, then Tirali's grey and white pattern), the three flagpoles and San Geminiano at the west end. The trapezoid plan is drawn as a rectangle.

landmarks.name: Procuratie Vecchie

dandolo-1204.name: Procuratie (Ziani's building)
dandolo-1204.note: A long two-storey Byzantine-style range of arcades built with Ziani's piazza, housing the Procurators of Saint Mark; Gentile Bellini painted it in 1496.

republic-1400.name: Procuratie (Ziani's building)
republic-1400.note: Still the old arcaded range with its crenellation, as in Gentile Bellini's Procession in the Piazza (1496). A fire in 1512 destroyed it.

cinquecento-1580.note: Rebuilt after the fire of 1512, from 1514 to about 1538: 50 arches below and two floors of arched windows above, under a crenellated cornice.

serenissima-1780.note: Apartments of the Procurators and rented shops; the Caffè Quadri opens under the arcades in 1775.

landmarks.summary: The long arcaded range on the north side of the Piazza, home and office of the Procurators of Saint Mark, the highest officers after the doge.
details: The Procurators administered the basilica, its treasure and countless charitable trusts. Their 12th-century building was rebuilt after the fire of 1512 by Bartolomeo Bon and Guglielmo dei Grigi, completed by Sansovino: 152 m of arcades, 50 below and 100 windows on each of the two upper floors.

The miniature shows the 16th-century range with its ground arcade, the two floors of round-headed windows and the white merlons on the cornice. The earlier variant, two storeys of Byzantine arches, follows Bellini's painting.
landmarks.function: Residences and offices of the Procurators of Saint Mark

landmarks.name: Procuratie Nuove

republic-1400.note: The site of the Hospice of Orseolo (founded 977) and a row of houses facing the Piazza.

cinquecento-1580.note: Being cleared for Vincenzo Scamozzi's new building (begun 1582), which will continue the order of Sansovino's Library along the south side of the Piazza.

serenissima-1780.note: Finished by Baldassare Longhena about 1640. Under its arcades the Caffè Florian has served coffee since 1720.

landmarks.summary: Scamozzi's three-storey classical range on the south side of the Piazza, begun in 1582 and finished about 1640, with the Caffè Florian under its arcades.
details: Designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi to continue the two orders of Sansovino's Library and to add a third, the building gave the Procurators new apartments and set the classical tone of the Piazza. After 1807 it became part of Napoleon's royal palace.
The miniature shows the three superimposed orders, Doric arcades, Ionic and Corinthian windows, under a cornice and a tiled roof.

landmarks.name: Torre dell'Orologio

republic-1400.note: The entrance to the Mercerie from the Piazza, among houses; the clock tower will be built over it in 1496–99.

cinquecento-1580.note: The clock tower of 1496–99, attributed to Mauro Codussi, with its gold and blue dial and the two bronze Moors striking the hours on the roof.

serenissima-1780.note: Giorgio Massari raised the side wings by a storey in 1755. At Epiphany and Ascension the Magi file out round the Madonna.

landmarks.summary: The clock tower over the gateway from the Piazza to the Mercerie (1496–99): a gold and blue dial of hours, signs and moon, the winged lion, and two bronze giants who strike the bell.
details: Built 1496–99 and attributed to Mauro Codussi, with the clockwork by Gian Paolo and Gian Carlo Rainieri of Reggio. The dial shows the hours in Roman numerals, the signs of the zodiac and the phases of the moon. The two bronze 'Moors' on the terrace were cast in 1497.
The miniature shows the tower with its arch, dial, Madonna, lion on a starry blue ground and the two bell-strikers, between the lower side wings.

landmarks.name: Libreria Marciana

republic-1400.note: Before the Library: hostelries and the stalls of bakers and butchers, cleared away for Sansovino's building.

cinquecento-1580.note: Sixteen bays stand, built by Sansovino from 1537 (the vault fell in 1545 and he was briefly jailed). The last five, toward the Molo, are added by Scamozzi in 1588–91.

serenissima-1780.note: Complete with its 21 bays. Inside, the library of Cardinal Bessarion and the ceiling roundels painted by Veronese and others.

landmarks.summary: Jacopo Sansovino's library (1537–88) facing the Doge's Palace across the Piazzetta: a Doric arcade below, an Ionic loggia of windows above, a balustrade of statues and obelisks.
details: Built to house the Greek and Latin manuscripts left to the Republic by Cardinal Bessarion in 1468, the Library brought Roman classical architecture to the heart of Venice. Palladio called it the richest building since antiquity. Sansovino built 16 bays; Vincenzo Scamozzi completed it in 1588–91.
The miniature shows the two orders with their arches, the deep frieze, and the balustrade with obelisks at the corners and statues above every column.

landmarks.name: Columns of San Marco and San Todaro

early-900.note: The harbour of the castle reached in here; the columns had not yet come.

dandolo-1204.note: Two granite columns from the east, raised on the Molo about 1172–77, traditionally by Nicolò Barattieri; the statues on top come later.

republic-1400.note: The winged bronze lion on the eastern column and Saint Theodore with his crocodile (set up in 1329) on the western one. Executions take place between them.

cinquecento-1580.note: The ceremonial gateway of the city from the sea: ambassadors and new doges landed here.

serenissima-1780.note: Unchanged; in Canaletto's views the gondolas wait at the Molo beneath them.

landmarks.summary: Two granite columns on the Molo, the sea gate of Venice, carrying the winged lion of Saint Mark and Saint Theodore, the city's first patron.
details: Brought from the eastern Mediterranean in the 12th century and raised about 1172–77; a third, by tradition, fell into the water and was never recovered. The bronze lion is a composite of uncertain, possibly ancient eastern, origin; Theodore is assembled from Roman fragments.
The miniature shows both columns on their stepped bases with their capitals and statues, scaled up slightly to read on the map.

landmarks.name: Bucintoro

dandolo-1204.note: A state barge for the doge is first mentioned in the 13th century; nothing is known of its form.

republic-1400.note: A Bucintoro ordered in 1311: a gilded galley with a covered deck for the doge and the Signoria, rowed out each Ascension Day for the Marriage of the Sea.

cinquecento-1580.note: The Bucintoro of 1526, gilded and carved, moored at the Molo on feast days and kept in its own shed in the Arsenal.

serenissima-1780.note: The last and grandest, launched in 1729 with carvings by Antonio Corradini: two decks, a red canopy and 168 rowers. The French burned it for its gold in 1798.

landmarks.summary: The doge's ceremonial galley, gilded from stem to stern, rowed out to the Lido every Ascension Day for the Marriage of the Sea.
details: On Ascension Day (the Sensa) the doge was rowed from the Molo to the port of San Nicolò and dropped a gold ring into the sea: 'We wed thee, sea, in sign of true and perpetual dominion.' Successive Bucintori were built in the Arsenal; the last, of 1729, was about 35 m long with 42 oars.

The miniature shows the 1729 ship moored at the Molo: lower deck of oars, the long red canopy over the upper deck, the figure of Justice at the prow and the doge's throne at the stern. Earlier ships are reconstructions.

landmarks.name: Ponte di Rialto

early-900.note: No bridge: boats ferried people across the Rivo Alto between the islets.

dandolo-1204.name: Ponte della Moneta
dandolo-1204.note: A bridge of boats laid about 1181, traditionally by Nicolò Barattieri, and named for the mint's tolls.

republic-1400.name: Ponte di Rialto (timber)
republic-1400.note: The timber bridge of the 1250s, with shops along both ramps and a central span that lifts for masted ships. Half burnt in 1310; it will collapse under a crowd in 1444.

cinquecento-1580.name: Ponte di Rialto (timber)
cinquecento-1580.note: Still the timber drawbridge painted by Carpaccio, rebuilt after the collapses of 1444 and 1524 and now rotten. The stone bridge follows in 1588–91.

serenissima-1780.note: Antonio da Ponte's stone bridge of 1588–91, chosen over designs by Palladio and others: one arch of 28.8 m carrying two rows of shops.

landmarks.summary: The only bridge across the Grand Canal until 1854: a bridge of boats, then a timber drawbridge lined with shops, and from 1591 a single stone arch.
details: The Rialto bridge joined the market to the Mercerie and San Marco. The timber bridge in Carpaccio's painting of 1496 had a central section that opened for ships. After a century of debate, the stone bridge was built in 1588–91 by Antonio da Ponte on 12,000 piles: one segmental arch, 7.5 m high, carrying three streets and two rows of shops.
The miniatures show the three bridges: the boats and planks, the timber ramps with shops and the lifting span, and the stone arch with its arcaded shops and central portico.

landmarks.name: Rialto market

early-900.note: The islet of Rivoalto: a landing beach, a few houses and the little church of San Giacomo, by tradition the oldest in Venice.

dandolo-1204.note: The public market since 1097, when the Orio family gave land here: stalls, warehouses and the banking tables round the church of San Giacomo.

republic-1400.note: The exchange of Europe and the Levant: bankers under the portico of San Giacomo, the loggia of the merchants, the fish and fruit markets by the water.

cinquecento-1580.note: Rebuilt after the great fire of January 1514: Scarpagnino's Fabbriche Vecchie (1520–22), the Camerlenghi palace, and Sansovino's Fabbriche Nuove (1554–56) along the canal.

serenissima-1780.note: Still the market for fish, fruit and vegetables; the public Banco del Giro (1619) keeps its books under the arcades.

landmarks.summary: The commercial heart of Venice on the west bank by the bridge: the church of San Giacomo, banks and magistracies, arcaded warehouses, and the fruit and fish markets on the Grand Canal.
details: Merchants met here every morning to settle accounts, insure cargoes and hear the news. After the fire of 1514 the state rebuilt the area as a regular complex of arcaded ranges round the campo: the Fabbriche Vecchie by Scarpagnino and, along the canal, the Fabbriche Nuove by Sansovino.

The miniature shows San Giacomo with its portico and great clock, the arcaded ranges, the Erberia stalls and the Pescheria loggia by the water. The earlier variant is a reconstruction with timber stalls and porticoes.

landmarks.name: Arsenale

early-900.note: Marshes and the twin islets of the Zemelle, where the Arsenal will be built.

dandolo-1204.name: Arsenale Vecchio
dandolo-1204.note: The first state shipyard, by tradition founded in 1104: a walled basin with covered slipways, where the galleys of the commune are built and stored. The rest is marsh.

republic-1400.name: Arsenale Vecchio and Nuovo
republic-1400.note: Doubled by the Arsenale Nuovo of about 1303–25. Dante (Inferno XXI) compared a pit of boiling pitch in Hell to the Arsenal's caulkers' cauldrons in winter.

cinquecento-1580.note: With the Arsenale Novissimo (from 1473), the Porta Magna (1460), the water gate towers (1574) and the new rope walk, the Tana, rebuilt from 1579: the largest industrial plant in Europe.

serenissima-1780.note: Past its peak but still building ships of the line; the lions brought from Piraeus by Francesco Morosini guard the gate since 1692. The French loot and burn it in 1797–98.

landmarks.summary: The state shipyard of the Republic: walled basins lined with covered slipways, rope walks, foundries and stores, where the galleys of the fleet were built and kept ready.
details: Traditionally founded in 1104 and enlarged in 1303–25 and again from 1473, the Arsenal covered about 45 ha behind its walls. In the 16th century it employed thousands of arsenalotti and could fit out a galley a day: in 1571 it sent a hundred galleys to Lepanto. Ships moved past the stores as on a production line.

The miniature shows the walls and towers, the Porta Magna and the water gate, the Darsena Vecchia, Nuova and Novissima with covered slipways (tese) and galleys, and the 316 m Tana along the south wall. The layout follows the de' Barbari view and later plans, simplified.

landmarks.name: Fondaco dei Tedeschi

dandolo-1204.note: Founded in 1228 as the warehouse and lodging of the German merchants, the state's way of watching and taxing their trade.

republic-1400.note: The old Fondaco: rooms and stores for the merchants of Nuremberg, Augsburg and Cologne round a court, with corner towers on the Grand Canal.

cinquecento-1580.note: Rebuilt after the fire of 1505 in 1505–08, its canal front painted with frescoes by Giorgione and its land front by Titian, now fading.

serenissima-1780.note: Still the Germans' house, with some 160 rooms; in 1806 it becomes the customs house.

landmarks.summary: The warehouse, market and hostel of the German merchants on the Grand Canal by the Rialto: four storeys of rooms round an arcaded court.
details: German merchants had to live, store and sell here, under Venetian officials who weighed their goods and took the duties. The building of 1505–08 has four storeys of arcaded galleries round a square court; its outer walls were frescoed by Giorgione and the young Titian.

The miniature shows the canal front with its five-arched portico and the corner turrets (removed in 1836), the rows of windows, the crenellation and the court. The fresco colour is a guess at its faded state.
landmarks.function: Warehouse and lodging of the German merchants

landmarks.name: Ca' d'Oro

dandolo-1204.note: The site of an older Zeno family palace on the Grand Canal.

republic-1400.note: Shown as built in 1421–c. 1434 for Marino Contarini, a little after this map's year; in 1400 the older Zeno house stood here.

cinquecento-1580.note: The Contarini palace, its gilding already worn: the most elaborate of the Gothic façades on the Grand Canal.

serenissima-1780.note: Passed through many owners and divided up; its staircase and wellhead will be sold off in the 19th century.

landmarks.summary: Marino Contarini's palace on the Grand Canal (1421–c. 1434), whose lace-like Gothic façade was once gilded and painted in ultramarine and vermilion.
details: Built by the Lombard Matteo Raverti and the Venetian Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bon, the 'house of gold' takes its name from the gilding of its tracery and ornaments. The façade is asymmetric: open loggias of interlaced arches and quatrefoils on the left, solid wall with windows on the right.
The miniature shows the water portico, the two traceried loggias, the cresting along the roofline and the house body behind with a court; colours follow the documented scheme loosely.

landmarks.name: Santi Giovanni e Paolo

dandolo-1204.note: Marshland given to the Dominican friars in 1234 by Doge Jacopo Tiepolo.

republic-1400.note: The great brick church of the Dominicans, begun about 1333, nearly finished; consecrated in 1430.

cinquecento-1580.note: The pantheon of the doges, 25 of whom are buried here; Verrocchio's bronze Colleoni (1488–96) rides in the campo.

serenissima-1780.note: Funerals of the doges are still held here, with the Scuola Grande di San Marco beside the façade.

landmarks.summary: The Dominican church of Venice (c. 1333–1430): a great brick Gothic hall church with tall apse windows and a dome over the crossing, burial place of the doges.
details: Zanipolo in Venetian, about 101 m long, built in brick with white stone trim. The façade was never finished above its marble portal. A lead dome with a lantern rises over the crossing.
The miniature shows the gabled front, the nave and aisles, the transept, the polygonal apses with lancet windows and the dome. Side chapels and the convent are left out.
landmarks.function: Dominican church and burial place of doges

landmarks.name: Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari

dandolo-1204.note: The Franciscans arrived about 1222 and were building their first church here from 1250.

republic-1400.note: The new church, begun about 1340 round the old one, is rising; the campanile, second in height only to San Marco's, was finished in 1396. Completed 1443.

cinquecento-1580.note: Titian's Assumption (1516–18) glows over the high altar; Titian himself was buried here in 1576, probably a victim of the plague.

serenissima-1780.note: The great Franciscan church, its convent now partly state archives in the making.

landmarks.summary: The Franciscan church of Venice (c. 1340–1443): an immense brick Gothic church with a 70 m campanile, home of Titian's Assumption.
details: Built by the Friars Minor in brick with Istrian stone trim, 102 m long, with a nave of huge round columns tied by timber beams and a marble choir screen in the middle. Its campanile (1361–96) is the second tallest in the city.
The miniature shows the gabled front with its pinnacles, the nave and aisles, the polygonal apse and chapels, and the campanile at the side of the choir. The orientation is approximate.

landmarks.name: San Giorgio Maggiore

early-900.note: A small church of Saint George on the island of cypresses; the Benedictines receive it in 982.

dandolo-1204.name: San Giorgio Maggiore (Benedictine abbey)
dandolo-1204.note: The Benedictine abbey church with its campanile and cloister; it holds the relics of Saint Stephen, brought from Constantinople in 1110.

republic-1400.name: San Giorgio Maggiore (Benedictine abbey)
republic-1400.note: The old basilica, rebuilt after the earthquake of 1223. Cosimo de' Medici, exiled to Venice in 1433, will pay for the monastery's library.

cinquecento-1580.note: Palladio's new church, begun in 1566, stands roofed and domed but without its marble façade, which is built only in 1607–11 after his death (August 1580).

serenissima-1780.note: Palladio's temple front faces San Marco across the basin. The old campanile collapsed in 1774; its replacement goes up only in 1791.

landmarks.summary: Palladio's Benedictine church on its island facing San Marco (1566–1610): a white temple front, a dome and, behind, the monastery.
details: Palladio solved the problem of putting a temple front on a church with aisles by interlocking two pediments: a tall one on four giant columns for the nave and a low, wide one for the aisles. The church was begun in 1566; the façade was completed in 1607–11.

The miniature shows the façade, nave, transept with apses, the dome and lantern, the choir and the monks' choir. The campanile is shown for 1580 and as a stump being rebuilt in 1780; the monastery is left to the map.

landmarks.name: Il Redentore

republic-1400.note: Gardens and houses along the Giudecca waterfront.

cinquecento-1580.note: Vowed by the Senate in September 1576 to end the plague; the foundation stone was laid on 3 May 1577. Walls rising inside scaffolding; consecrated 1592.

serenissima-1780.note: The Capuchins' church, goal of the yearly Redentore procession on the third Sunday of July over a bridge of boats from the Zattere.

landmarks.summary: Palladio's votive church on the Giudecca (1577–92), built to thank Christ the Redeemer for the end of the plague of 1575–77.
details: The Senate vowed the church in 1576 when the plague had killed perhaps a quarter of the city. Palladio designed a long nave with side chapels leading to a domed space and a choir screened by columns, for the Capuchin friars; a broad stair climbs to the white temple front.
The miniature shows the façade, the nave and chapels, the high dome between two slim round bell towers and the choir. The 1580 variant shows the walls going up, a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Santa Maria della Salute

republic-1400.note: The Trinità church and the house of the Teutonic Knights stood at the Punta della Dogana.

cinquecento-1580.note: Warehouses, the Trinità and a seminary. The plague of 1630–31, which kills about a third of the city, will bring the vow to build the Salute here.

serenissima-1780.note: Longhena's votive church (1631–87), with the Dogana da Mar (1677–82) at the point beyond. Every 21 November the city crosses a bridge of boats to give thanks.

landmarks.summary: Baldassare Longhena's votive church at the mouth of the Grand Canal (1631–87): an octagon with a great dome on giant scroll buttresses, a second dome and two bell towers behind.
details: Vowed by the Senate in October 1630 at the height of the plague and dedicated to the Virgin of health, the church stands on a platform of more than a million wooden piles, by tradition. Longhena's octagon has six chapels and a triumphal-arch entrance; giant volutes, the orecchioni ('big ears'), buttress the drum.
The miniature shows the steps, the entrance front, the chapels, the volutes with their statues, the great dome and lantern with the Virgin, the sanctuary dome and the two campanili.

landmarks.name: Ghetto Nuovo

republic-1400.note: An islet of the public copper foundry (getto), where cannon and bronze were cast; the name Ghetto comes from it.

cinquecento-1580.note: Since 29 March 1516 the Jews of Venice must live here, behind gates locked at night. Ashkenazi synagogues (1528, 1532, 1575) sit on the top floors; pawnbanks under the arcades.

serenissima-1780.note: Houses of seven and eight storeys, the tallest in Venice, for some 1,600 people in decline. Napoleon's troops will burn the gates in July 1797.

landmarks.summary: The walled island where the Jews of Venice were made to live from 1516, the first ghetto: a campo with wellheads ringed by the tallest houses of the city, with synagogues hidden on their top floors.
details: The Senate's decree of 29 March 1516 confined the Jews to the Ghetto Nuovo, an island reached by two bridges with gates guarded by Christians paid by the community. The Ghetto Vecchio (1541) and Nuovissimo (1633) were added. With no room to spread, houses rose to seven or eight storeys with low ceilings.

The miniature shows the campo and its three wellheads, the ring of tall houses, the gates on the bridges, the five windows of the Scola Grande Tedesca and the little cupola of the Scola Canton on the roofs.

landmarks.name: San Pietro di Castello

early-900.name: San Pietro di Olivolo
early-900.note: The bishop's church of Olivolo, seat of the bishops of Venice since about 775, on its own island at the east end of the city.

dandolo-1204.name: San Pietro di Castello
dandolo-1204.note: The cathedral, far from the doge's church; the bishops of Castello and the doges kept their distance.

republic-1400.note: Since 1451 the seat of the Patriarch of Venice, still a long Romanesque basilica with a brick campanile.

cinquecento-1580.note: Mauro Codussi's campanile of white Istrian stone (1482–90) stands apart from the old church; Palladio's façade, designed in 1558, is built only in 1594–96.

serenissima-1780.note: The patriarchal cathedral with Palladio's façade and Codussi's campanile; it stays the cathedral until 1807, when the patriarch moves to San Marco.

landmarks.summary: The cathedral of Venice until 1807, on the island of Olivolo at the city's eastern end, with Palladio's white front and Codussi's stone campanile.
details: The bishopric of Olivolo, later Castello, dates from about 775. The cathedral's remoteness from San Marco expressed the distance between Church and State in Venice. The present church follows Palladio's design of 1558, built in 1594–96, and was remodelled inside in the 17th century.
The miniature shows the Palladian front, nave, dome and apse, and Codussi's campanile across the campo. The older basilica is a reconstruction.
landmarks.function: Cathedral of the bishops and patriarchs of Venice

spots.name: The landing at Rivoalto
spots.summary: The beach and wooden landing stages on the Rivo Alto where boats from the mainland and the lagoon unloaded wine, grain, timber and salt: the seed of the Rialto market.
details: Rivoalto, the 'high bank', was the firmest ground in the archipelago, which is why the doges moved here in 810–811. Its landing became the natural market: a document of 1097 records the Orio family giving land by the canal for a public market.

vignettes.text: Flat-bottomed barges from the rivers nose onto the mud. Men in short tunics wade out with sacks of grain on their shoulders; a priest blesses the first salt boat of the season.
Fishermen spread eels and grey mullet on wet reeds. Mainland peasants bring eggs and cheese; a lagoon boatman haggles in coin from the mint of Pavia.
The tide comes up over the landing planks. Boats are dragged onto the bank and turned over; smoke and the smell of fried fish drift from the timber houses.

dandolo-1204.name: Rialto landings
dandolo-1204.note: The landings are now quays of the market, with the bridge of boats just upstream and warehouses of the merchants along the bank.

spots.name: Salt pans of the northern marsh
spots.summary: Shallow pans cut into the barene, where lagoon water was let in and evaporated by the summer sun: salt was the first fortune of the Venetians.
details: Cassiodorus wrote in the 6th century that the lagoon people had no wealth but fish and salt, and that salt was worth more than gold to them. Saltworks ringed the lagoon in the 9th and 10th centuries; Venice later controlled the salt of Chioggia and taxed salt throughout its trade.

vignettes.text: The salt-workers open a sluice and the morning tide slides into the first pan, grey and shallow. Herons stalk the dykes between the pans.
White crust shines in the pans under a hard sun. Barefoot workers rake it into heaps with wooden rakes; the heaps are covered with reeds against rain.
Boats load sacks of salt for the river towns. The marsh smells of brine and rotting weed; mosquitoes rise from the creeks.

spots.name: San Nicolò dei Mendicoli
spots.summary: The fishermen's church at the western tip of Dorsoduro, one of the oldest in the city, whose parishioners, the Nicolotti, elected their own 'doge' and fought the Castellani.
details: Founded, by tradition, in the 7th century and rebuilt in the 12th, San Nicolò served a poor parish of fishermen and boatmen. The Nicolotti had their own gastaldo, the doge dei Nicolotti, received by the real doge, and with the Castellani of the east end they formed the two factions of the city's popular games.

vignettes.text: Fishermen in brown woollen caps step out of low houses to their boats, nets heaped in the bows. The church door is open; a candle burns before the image of Saint Nicholas.
Women mend nets along the canal and gut the morning's catch. Children dive off the fondamenta; a boat of reeds for thatching ties up.
The men come home to soup and polenta. In the campo the talk is of the next battle on the bridges with the Castellani.

early-900.note: A small church on the edge of the marsh, its parish the fishermen of the western islets.

serenissima-1780.note: The Nicolotti still elect their doge, who is received in state at the Doge's Palace.

spots.name: Glassmakers of Rialto
spots.summary: A glass furnace in the city: until 1291 the glassmakers worked here among the houses; then fear of fire sent their furnaces to Murano and the shops stayed in town.
details: A glassmaker, a 'phiolarius', is named in a Venetian document of 982. The guild's statute dates from 1271, and in 1291 the Great Council ordered all furnaces out of the city to Murano because of the risk of fire. Venice guarded the craft's secrets jealously; glassmakers who emigrated could be pursued.

vignettes.text: The furnace has burned all night. A boy feeds it alder wood while the master gathers a glowing blob on his iron pipe and blows a bubble of green glass.
Lamps, bottles and beads cool in the annealing oven. A neighbour complains of the heat and the sparks over the shingle roofs.
The fire is banked, never put out. The glassmakers drink in the yard; the glow from the furnace mouth lights their faces.

republic-1400.name: Glass shop at Rialto
republic-1400.note: The furnaces went to Murano in 1291. Here a shop sells Murano beads, cups and lamps; the glassblowers come over by boat.

cinquecento-1580.name: Glass shop at Rialto
cinquecento-1580.note: Murano mirrors and crystal (cristallo, clear as rock crystal) are luxuries sold across Europe.

serenissima-1780.name: Glass shop at Rialto
serenissima-1780.note: Bohemian glass competes; Murano answers with chandeliers and coloured beads for the Africa trade.

spots.name: Spice merchant's warehouse
spots.summary: A spice merchant's storehouse near the Rialto: pepper, ginger, cinnamon and cloves from the convoys of Alexandria and Beirut, weighed, sorted and sold on to the Germans.
details: The state galley convoys to Alexandria and Beirut brought spices bought from Arab merchants; Venice resold them to buyers from Germany and the north. The Portuguese route round Africa (1498) cut into the trade, but Venetian spice imports recovered by the mid-16th century.

vignettes.text: The galleys from Alexandria are in. Porters stagger up from the barges with sacks of pepper; clerks tally them in a ledger by the door.
A buyer from Nuremberg bites a clove, sniffs the ginger, argues over the price in bad Italian. Sieves shake the dust out of the pepper.
The doors are barred. The whole calle smells of cinnamon; the merchant counts his ducats by lamplight.

spots.name: Bankers of Rialto
spots.summary: The banking tables under the portico of San Giacomo di Rialto, where merchants paid each other by transfer in the banker's book instead of in coin.
details: The banchi di scritta kept accounts for merchants: a payment was made by both parties standing before the banker as he wrote the transfer in his book. Private banks failed often; in 1587 the state founded the Banco della Piazza di Rialto and in 1619 the Banco del Giro.

vignettes.text: The bell of San Giacomo rings for the opening. Merchants in black gowns crowd the tables; the banker dips his pen and writes 'by order of'.
News from Syria: a ship is lost. Voices rise; insurers gather in the corner of the portico, and a merchant checks his balance twice.
Accounts are closed, the books locked in an iron-bound chest. The campo empties of everyone but the porters and the pigeons.

serenissima-1780.name: Banco del Giro
serenissima-1780.note: The public transfer bank of 1619 keeps the merchants' accounts in bank money worth more than coin.

spots.name: Fish market at Rialto
spots.summary: The fish market on the Grand Canal by the Rialto, where the catch of the lagoon and the Adriatic was sold every morning under the eye of the state's fish officials.
details: Fish could be sold only at Rialto and San Marco, at prices and in sizes fixed by the Giustizia Vecchia. A marble plaque gave the minimum length of each species. The fishermen of San Nicolò had special rights to sell their own catch.

vignettes.text: Boats from Chioggia unload baskets of sole, mullet, cuttlefish and live eels. The officials walk the benches with their measuring rods.
Cooks of patrician houses pick over the best turbot; a fishwife shouts that her sardines jumped this morning. Water runs everywhere.
Benches are scrubbed and doused. Gulls fight over the heads and guts thrown into the canal.

spots.name: Squero of San Trovaso
spots.summary: A boatyard on the Rio di San Trovaso, where gondolas and other lagoon boats were built and repaired on a slipway in front of a timber house.
details: Squeri lined the canals at the edge of the city. The gondola took its familiar asymmetric form only slowly; a law of 1562 required them to be black. Builders, often from the Cadore mountains, used eight kinds of wood: oak, elm, larch, fir, cherry, walnut, lime and mahogany in later centuries.

vignettes.text: A gondola lies keel-up on the ramp. The master lights a fire of reeds under the hull to bend the planks, and pitch bubbles in a pot.
Apprentices plane oak ribs in the shade of the wooden house; geraniums hang from its balcony. A boatman waits to have his boat re-tarred.
The finished boat slides down the ramp into the rio and floats. The workmen cross to the Zattere for a glass of wine.

republic-1400.note: A boatyard building and repairing lagoon boats of many shapes; the gondola is still a light, plain, often coloured craft.

serenissima-1780.note: Black gondolas with their steel prow (ferro) and the cabin (felze) for winter and secrecy.

spots.name: Traghetto of San Tomà
spots.summary: A gondola ferry across the Grand Canal, run by a guild of boatmen who held the crossing as a monopoly and kept their own altar and rules.
details: With only one bridge over the Grand Canal, the traghetti carried people across at a dozen points. Each was a scuola of boatmen with statutes (mariegole) fixing fares and turns. The crossing at San Tomà is one of the oldest.

vignettes.text: Servants with baskets, a notary with his papers and a priest stand in the boat; the gondolier pushes off and calls the far side.
The boatmen play cards on the steps between crossings, arguing whose turn it is. A coin falls into the water and nobody dives for it.
Lanterns on the landing. A masked couple wants to cross; the gondolier asks no names.

spots.name: Wellhead of Santa Maria Formosa
spots.summary: A carved stone wellhead in the campo of Santa Maria Formosa, the mouth of a cistern that collected rain filtered through sand: the city's only fresh water besides boats from the mainland.
details: Under each campo a clay-lined pit filled with sand filtered rainwater from the paving into a central brick shaft. The wellheads were locked and opened twice a day by the parish. In droughts boats of the acquaroli brought water from the Brenta river.

vignettes.text: The parish keeper unlocks the iron lid. Women with copper buckets on yokes queue and gossip; the first bucket comes up cold and clear.
Children splash each other at the wellhead; a water-seller fills his casks for houses far from any well. The campo smells of drying laundry.
The keeper locks the lid again. Rain begins and the gratings in the paving gurgle as the cistern drinks.

early-900.note: A plain cistern and well by the church of Santa Maria Formosa, founded according to tradition in the 7th century.

spots.name: Ospedale della Pietà
spots.summary: The foundling hospital on the Riva degli Schiavoni whose girls, trained in music, became the most famous orchestra and choir in Europe; Vivaldi taught here.
details: Founded in 1346, the Pietà took in abandoned babies through a hatch in its wall. The most gifted girls, the figlie di coro, sang and played behind iron grilles for paying visitors. Antonio Vivaldi was its violin master and composer, off and on, from 1703 to 1740.

vignettes.text: A bundle is left at the scaffetta, the little hatch in the wall, with half a medal tied to it so that the mother might one day claim the child.
Violins practise scales behind the shutters. A girl of fourteen repeats a passage ten times while the maestra taps the beat.
Vespers: visitors fill the church to hear the invisible choir behind the grilles. Foreigners swear the singers must be angels.

republic-1400.note: A new charity for foundlings, run by a confraternity; music comes later.

cinquecento-1580.note: Hundreds of children; the girls learn crafts and music, and the choir begins to draw listeners.

spots.name: Aldine Press
spots.summary: The printing house founded by Aldus Manutius about 1494 near Sant'Agostin, which printed the Greek classics, invented the pocket book and the italic type.
details: Aldus came to Venice about 1490 and from 1494 printed Aristotle, Plato and the Greek poets with scholars from Crete and Constantinople. His octavo classics of 1501 in Francesco Griffo's italic made books portable. His heirs ran the press until 1597; Venice was Europe's capital of printing.

vignettes.text: Compositors pick metal letters from the cases, Greek on one side, italic on the other. A Cretan scholar checks yesterday's proofs for accents.
The press thumps; damp sheets hang drying on lines across the room. A sign on the door asks visitors to state their business and leave quickly.
Ink-black apprentices wash at the canal. In the shop a young patrician buys a pocket Virgil to read in his gondola.

cinquecento-1580.note: Run by Aldus's grandson Aldo the Younger; the dolphin and anchor mark is still on Venetian books.

spots.name: Scuola Grande di San Rocco
spots.summary: One of the great lay confraternities of Venice, devoted to the plague saint Roch, whose hall Tintoretto covered with more than fifty paintings.
details: The six scuole grandi were brotherhoods of citizens and craftsmen who ran charity, processions and their members' funerals. San Rocco's building (1517–60) by Bartolomeo Bon the Younger and Scarpagnino was decorated by Tintoretto from 1564 to 1588.

vignettes.text: The brothers in white habits gather for Mass on the saint's feast. Alms are handed out to widows queuing at the door.
Tintoretto's assistants carry a huge canvas up the stairs; the guardian grande inspects the gold of the ceiling frames.
The chapter votes dowries for poor girls with balls of linen dropped into a box. Outside, the campo smells of the Frari's incense.

cinquecento-1580.note: Tintoretto is at work on the upper hall; the plague of 1575–77 makes Saint Roch's brotherhood busier than ever.

spots.name: Battle on the Ponte dei Pugni
spots.summary: The bridge of San Barnaba without parapets, where the Castellani and the Nicolotti fought each other with fists for possession of the bridge, before crowds of thousands.
details: From the 14th century the two factions of working Venice met on bridges each autumn, first with sticks, later with fists. The battles drew patricians and foreign princes; losers went into the canal. The state tolerated them until a bloody fight in 1705.

vignettes.text: Boys of each side taunt each other across the bridge. Boatmen moor their boats along the rio and rent the seats to spectators.
The champions advance to the marble footprints at the top. A blow, a roar, and three Castellani topple into the water.
The Nicolotti hold the bridge and carry their champion home. Wine is poured at San Nicolò; bruises are counted.

spots.name: Mask maker's shop
spots.summary: A shop of the mascareri near San Zulian, where masks of papier-mâché and waxed cloth were made for Carnival and for anonymity all year round.
details: Mask makers had their own guild statute from 1436. In the 18th century masks were worn for months: from October to Lent, at Ascension and at many festivals. The bauta, a white mask with a black tricorn and cloak, let nobles and commoners mix unrecognised.

vignettes.text: Wet paper strips are laid over clay moulds of faces. A row of white bautas dries on a shelf by the window.
A servant buys a moretta, the black oval mask held by a button in the teeth, for his mistress. Gold paint dries on a Columbina.
The shop is still open: late customers want a mask for the theatre. Outside, a masked crowd flows toward the Piazza.

cinquecento-1580.note: Carnival masks, and masks for the theatre of the commedia dell'arte, now popular in the city.

spots.name: Caffè Florian
spots.summary: The coffee house under the arcades of the Procuratie Nuove, opened by Floriano Francesconi in 1720 as 'Alla Venezia Trionfante', the meeting place of all Venice.
details: Coffee came to Venice in the 17th century and by the 18th there were dozens of coffee houses round the Piazza. Florian's was one of the few that admitted women; Goldoni, Casanova and later Byron and Goethe's contemporaries went there.

vignettes.text: A waiter in a white apron carries chocolate to a patrician still in last night's mask. Newspapers from Amsterdam lie on the marble tables.
Talk of the latest Goldoni play, a scandal at the Ridotto, the price of grain. A charlatan's drum sounds from the Piazza.
Candles in the little rooms; the Piazza is full of masks and music. Nobody here is going home before dawn.

spots.name: Public bakeries of the Arsenal
spots.summary: The state ovens on the Riva by the Arsenal's canal, which baked biscotto, the twice-baked ship's biscuit that fed the crews of the galleys.
details: The Forni Pubblici (rebuilt 1473) baked hard biscuit that kept for months at sea and was stored in the Arsenal for the fleet. Rowers on a galley ate about half a kilo of it a day, with wine, cheese and beans.

vignettes.text: The ovens have been lit since midnight. Bakers knead dough of wheat and water only, no salt; the loaves go in twice.
Sacks of biscuit are stacked to the ceiling and carted to the Arsenal stores. Sparrows hop under the barrows.
A galley's purser signs for biscuit for 200 men for a month. The Riva smells of bread and tar.

spots.name: Salt warehouses of the Zattere
spots.summary: The state warehouses where the salt of Chioggia and the Mediterranean was stored and taxed, along the quay facing the Giudecca.
details: Salt was a state monopoly and one of the Republic's largest revenues. The Magazzini del Sale held tens of thousands of tonnes; the Salt Office (Ufficio del Sal) also funded public building, including the stone Rialto bridge.

vignettes.text: A salt barge from Chioggia ties up. Porters with baskets on their heads trot up the plank into the long dim hall.
Clerks of the Salt Office weigh and stamp each load. White dust coats everything; the men's eyes sting.
The great doors close and are sealed. Rafts of timber from the Alps knock against the quay in the dusk.

events.title: The body of Saint Mark comes to Venice
events.text: Two Venetian merchants, Buono of Malamocco and Rustico of Torcello, took the body of the evangelist from his church in Alexandria and smuggled it aboard under a load of pork, which Muslim customs men would not touch. Doge Giustiniano Partecipazio received it; a chapel was built beside his castle to keep it, and the lion of Mark became the city's sign.

events.title: Revolt: the palace and San Marco burn
events.text: The people rose against Doge Pietro IV Candiano, who ruled like a feudal prince. They set fire to houses next to his castle; the fire spread to the palace, San Marco and, the chroniclers say, some 300 houses. The doge was killed trying to escape with his infant son. His successor Pietro I Orseolo rebuilt both at his own cost.

events.title: Emperor and Pope reconciled at San Marco
events.text: After eighteen years of schism, Emperor Frederick Barbarossa knelt before Pope Alexander III at the door of San Marco and kissed his foot. Venice had brokered the peace and staged it; later legend said the grateful pope gave the doge the ring with which to marry the sea.

events.title: The Fourth Crusade sails
events.text: The crusaders could not pay for the fleet Venice had built for them, so Doge Enrico Dandolo, old and nearly blind, took the cross in San Marco and led it himself. The fleet of galleys, horse transports and round ships sailed past the Lido with trumpets sounding. It went first to Zara, then to Constantinople, which it sacked in 1204.

events.title: The Tiepolo conspiracy fails at the Rialto
events.text: Bajamonte Tiepolo and the Querini led an armed rising against the doge. In the Merceria a woman dropped a stone mortar from her window, killing the rebels' standard-bearer; the column broke and fled back over the Rialto, burning the timber bridge behind it. To watch for plots the Council of Ten was created, at first for a few months.

events.title: The Black Death
events.text: The plague arrived early in 1348 on ships from the east. Within months perhaps half the city was dead. The Great Council named three officials to bury the dead on outlying islands and to keep order; it was the beginning of the health magistracy that later invented quarantine on the lagoon islands.

events.title: War of Chioggia: the last galleys
events.text: In August 1379 the Genoese took Chioggia at the south end of the lagoon. The people demanded the release of the admiral Vettor Pisani from prison; patricians and commoners paid and rowed for new galleys built in the Arsenal. Venice blockaded the Genoese in Chioggia, and they surrendered in June 1380.

events.title: The Jews are confined to the Ghetto
events.text: The Senate ordered all Jews in the city to live on the island of the old foundry, the Ghetto Nuovo. Two gates were locked at night and guarded by Christians paid by the community; Jews had to wear a yellow badge or hat by day. It was segregation, but also a legal right to live in Venice.

events.title: News of Lepanto
events.text: The galley Angelo Gabriele rowed into the basin trailing captured Turkish banners in the water: the Holy League had destroyed the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto on 7 October, more than a hundred of its galleys from Venice's Arsenal. Bells rang for days; shops closed, and the Piazza was lit and hung with Turkish trophies.

events.title: Henri III sees a galley built
events.text: Henri of Valois, on his way from Poland to be crowned king of France, was given ten days of festivities. At the Arsenal, the story goes, the workers assembled and launched a galley from ready-made parts while he ate a banquet; at Murano glassblowers worked on a raft beside his gondola.

events.title: The plague ends: the first Redentore
events.text: When the plague that had killed perhaps a quarter of the city was declared over, the doge, the Senate and the people crossed the Giudecca canal on a bridge of boats to the site of the church vowed to Christ the Redeemer, its walls barely begun. The procession has been repeated on the third Sunday of July ever since.

events.title: Fire in the Doge's Palace
events.text: A fire swept through the halls of the Great Council and the Scrutinio, destroying paintings by Guariento, Gentile and Giovanni Bellini, Carpaccio and Titian. Some wanted the Gothic palace rebuilt in the modern style; the Senate chose to restore it as it was, and Tintoretto, Veronese and Palma painted the new ceilings and walls.

events.title: The Marriage of the Sea
events.text: The doge boarded the Bucintoro at the Molo and was rowed out to the port of San Nicolò at the Lido, followed by hundreds of boats. There he dropped a gold ring into the water: 'We wed thee, sea, in sign of true and perpetual dominion.' A fair filled the Piazza for two weeks and the city stayed masked.

events.title: The Republic votes itself out of existence
events.text: With Napoleon's army on the lagoon shore, the Great Council, short of a quorum and hearing gunfire it took for an attack, voted to hand power to a provisional municipality. Doge Ludovico Manin, it is said, took off his cap of office and gave it to his valet: he would not need it again. After 1,100 years the Republic was over.

stories.title: A merchant's morning at the Rialto
stories.summary: Follow a Venetian merchant through a spring morning in 1400 as the Alexandria galleys come in: the banks, the Germans' house, the spice store, the bridge, the palace and San Marco.

steps.title: At the banker's table
steps.text: Under the portico of San Giacomo you stand before your banker with a Florentine wool dealer while the banker writes the transfer in his book: no coin changes hands. The bell of San Giacomo rings the start of business.

steps.title: News at the Rialto
steps.text: In the campo everyone has heard: the galleys from Alexandria are past the Lido. Pepper prices are already falling. Insurers huddle by the loggia; a broker offers you a share in the Flanders voyage.

steps.title: Pepper in the store
steps.text: Your factor opens the warehouse and shows the sacks of last year's pepper and ginger. You decide to hold the ginger and sell the pepper before the new cargo lands.

steps.title: Selling to the Germans
steps.text: Across the bridge, in the Germans' house, a merchant of Nuremberg buys your pepper for silver. A Venetian broker, the only one allowed to deal with him, takes his fee and the clerk of the office his duty.

steps.title: Over the timber bridge
steps.text: You cross back over the Rialto bridge among porters and shop counters; the drawbridge in the middle is down today. Boats queue below for the ships' cargo.

steps.title: A petition at the palace
steps.text: At the palace you wait in the arcade with a petition for an export licence. Above you the new hall of the Great Council is nearly finished; masons are carving the balcony window.

steps.title: Thanks in San Marco
steps.text: You light a candle to Saint Mark for the safe return of the galleys. The gold of the domes glows in the lamplight; outside, the horses look down on the Piazza.

stories.title: A night of Carnival, 1780
stories.summary: A masked evening in the last years of the Republic, from the mask maker's shop to coffee on the Piazza, music at the Pietà and a gondola across the Grand Canal to the Salute.

steps.title: Choosing a mask
steps.text: You buy a bauta, the white mask with its black hood and tricorn: in it nobody can tell a patrician from a gondolier, a nun from a duchess. The shopkeeper ties it on and wishes you luck.

steps.title: The Piazza at night
steps.text: Lanterns, puppet booths, a tightrope walker strung from the campanile, mountebanks selling cures. Everyone is masked and everyone greets you as 'Siora Maschera'.

steps.title: Chocolate at Florian's
steps.text: Under the arcades of the Procuratie Nuove you take chocolate in a little mirrored room. A masked lady at the next table seems to know everything about you.

steps.title: The invisible choir
steps.text: On the Riva the church of the Pietà is full: behind the grilles the foundling girls play a concerto. Visitors argue whether the soloist is fifteen or fifty; no one will ever see her face.

steps.title: Across the Grand Canal
steps.text: A gondolier with a lantern takes you across at San Tomà. He sings a verse of Tasso to a boatman on the far bank, who answers with the next.

steps.title: Dawn at the Salute
steps.text: You end the night on the steps of the Salute, the domes grey against the sky, the first boats rowing out to the market. In seventeen years the Republic will be gone.
